title: Modern and Mexican: Mario Pani’s CUPA Housing Complex in Mexico City
text:
Modern and Mexican: Mario Pani’s CUPA Housing Complex in Mexico City

In 1947, Mexico's General Directorate of Civil Pensions commissioned young architect Mario Pani to design 200 houses for government employees on a recently acquired plot of land in Colonia del Valle, then a distant neighborhood on the outskirts of Mexico City. Rather than following the original guidelines, Pani proposed a 13-story housing complex with extensive green areas, communal spaces, and more than a thousand apartments. Drawing on Le Corbusier's functionalist principles, the architect created a project that opened in 1949 and would become a landmark in Latin American modern architecture.

title: The Cloud House / Peter Morris Architects
text:
The Cloud House / Peter Morris Architects

Architect Peter Morris reveals his most remarkable achievement to date: 'The Cloud House'. Drawing inspiration from the eccentric, Grade I-listed St Martin's Church opposite, and the castle-like Grade II-listed school next door, the property brings a touch of fairytale flamboyance to its north London surroundings. Its pale-pink exteriors, oversized arches, and duck-egg blue metalwork bring joyfulness and colour to the eclectic local architecture, with an interior featuring pale turquoise painted epoxy floors, pink and white marquee stripes on walls and ceilings, and an emerald green and white striped kitchen with pale pink Plykea worktops.

title: The Nordic Pavilion Explores Traditional Craft Through "Painted Matter" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
text:
The Nordic Pavilion Explores Traditional Craft Through "Painted Matter" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

The National Museum of Norway has announced Painted Matter as the title of Norway's contribution to the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of the Venice Biennale, scheduled to take place from May 8 to November 21, 2027. Developed by Oslo-based practice Kastler Skjeseth Architects, the exhibition will be presented at the Nordic Pavilion and will explore the role of traditional decorative painting techniques in contemporary architecture, with a focus on material use, architectural expression, and sustainability. The Nordic Pavilion, designed by Norwegian architect Sverre Fehn, is jointly owned by Norway, Sweden, and Finland. For the 2027 edition, the National Museum of Norway is responsible for organizing the Nordic contribution on behalf of Moderna Museet in Stockholm and the Architecture and Design Museum in Helsinki.

title: UN-Habitat and ICPAC Launch a Practical Guide to Help Cities Prepare for El Niño
text:
UN-Habitat and ICPAC Launch a Practical Guide to Help Cities Prepare for El Niño

El Niño is a natural climate pattern expected to peak from October 2026 through March 2027. It is characterized by a strong impact on global weather patterns, bringing floods, droughts, heat waves and storms to different regions. On November 5, 2026, the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) and the Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) launched a short practical guide for city governments to help them prepare for the upcoming season. The guide offers considerations applicable to different climate regions, but it is framed by IGAD in the context of preparedness, anticipatory action and resilience in the Horn of Africa (Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan and Uganda). Its aim is to offer actionable guidance to improve urban resilience, protect vulnerable communities and reduce the impacts of climate-related hazards.

title: Miami Architecture City Guide: 22 Projects Shaping Tropical Density on the Atlantic Coast
text:
Miami Architecture City Guide: 22 Projects Shaping Tropical Density on the Atlantic Coast

Stretching along the Atlantic coast at the southern tip of Florida, Miami is often introduced through postcard views of beaches, palm trees, and glass towers facing the water. Yet, behind this familiar image lies a city shaped by migration, tourism, and real estate cycles, where architecture has repeatedly been used to project new identities and reinvent the urban landscape. From early resort hotels and the Art Deco façades of South Beach to experimental high-rises and cultural institutions on the bay, the built environment offers a way to read how Miami negotiates climate, economy, and everyday life.

title: Verra / MVRDV
text:
Verra / MVRDV

MVRDV has completed construction of Verra, a residential complex providing 343 apartments at the new Enterprise Research Campus (ERC) in Boston. Surrounded by a mixture of laboratories, conference facilities, and a hotel, Verra's ground floor layer of locally owned shops, cafés, and restaurants help to integrate it into Allstonway, the new public park that forms the central spine of the ERC. The project thus places residents at the heart of a vibrant district that brings together the international science and innovation community with the Allston-Brighton community. Meanwhile, behind the green façade a diverse collection of apartments offer expansive views through the design's many corner windows, giving residents a high quality of life both at home and out in the neighbourhood.

title: Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA Receives the First Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture
text:
Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA Receives the First Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture

The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) has selected Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA as the recipient of the first Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture. The prize goes to the Dhaka-based architectural office for the design of the Friendship Centre, a rural training facility in Gaibandha, Bangladesh, inspired by one of the country's oldest urban archaeological sites. The prize, which MoMA describes as the largest award for a single architecture project, aims to recognize architectural practice while supporting tangible environmental action. Eligible projects may have been completed anywhere in the world in the past 30 years and must be considered exemplary in repairing architecture's relationship with nature. On this occasion, the $200,000 award is shared between the architect and the Fundación Gran Chaco, a nonprofit organization in Formosa, Argentina, which will plant trees in the Gran Chaco forest in the name of the project's client, the Friendship NGO, to contribute to reforestation efforts.

title: From Source to Site: How Recovered and Engineered Materials Shape Design
text:
From Source to Site: How Recovered and Engineered Materials Shape Design

Conventional construction often begins with a specification: a particular brick, concrete mix, manufactured panel or finish selected for a proposed building. What changes when the design process begins with a material that has already been recovered, produced or made available? Today, projects approach material resources through different processes: recovery, recycling and the engineering of locally sourced bamboo. Taken together, the varied approaches will show how material sourcing and processing can influence architectural decisions before a product reaches the building site.

title: Brazil in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Cultural Heritage and Climate Resilience
text:
Brazil in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Cultural Heritage and Climate Resilience

Architecture in Brazil this month brings questions of cultural identity, environmental resilience, and the relationship between architecture and territory into focus. Across the country, recent developments reflect different ways of understanding and responding to the conditions that shape the built environment, from the role of architecture in preserving collective memory to the challenges of adapting cities to environmental change. From cultural and public projects to heritage initiatives and new institutional developments, this month's selection explores how architecture responds to the evolving needs and identities of places and the communities that inhabit them.

text:

Continuing the site's connection to maritime trade, the project brings together restored industrial buildings, spaces for collaboration, and a landscape designed to support local biodiversity.

title: From the Fun Palace to the Fish: Architecture’s Triumph or Computation’s Takeover?
text:
From the Fun Palace to the Fish: Architecture’s Triumph or Computation’s Takeover?

The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan, rises in fluid curves and folds in the midst of a wide clearing in the city's gridded forest of urban blocks. The striking structure, completed in 2013 by Zaha Hadid Architects, acts as a primary venue for the country's cultural programs. Its curvaceous form sits in contrast to its rectilinear surroundings, marking its importance. The carefully curated curves epitomize a constant ambition in the studio's work–to dissolve the distinction between the horizontal and the vertical, between inside and outside, and between landscape and building. Needless to say, its complexity marks it as a feat of construction as well as of architecture. As Zaha Hadid Architects note, "Advanced computing allowed for the continuous control and communication of these complexities among the numerous project participants." Indeed, it is computing that made the building of the center possible, as well as other projects by the studio. As architecture becomes increasingly entangled with the digital realm, one can even ask if this is a triumph of the discipline or that of computation.
